title: “The Lord hath created a new thing in the earth, A woman shall compass a man” — what is the new thing?
summary: Jeremiah 31:22 says the Lord “hath created a new thing in the earth” and gives it as “A woman shall compass a man”. The verse does not say in what way the thing is new or what it is for.
text: KJV Jeremiah 31:21: “Set thee up waymarks, make thee high heaps: set thine heart toward the highway, even the way which thou wentest: turn again, O virgin of Israel, turn again to these thy cities.” KJV Jeremiah 31:22: “How long wilt thou go about, O thou backsliding daughter? for the Lord hath created a new thing in the earth, A woman shall compass a man.”
reasoning: The verse names the thing as an act, “A woman shall compass a man”, without saying what the act means, who the woman and the man are, or what is new in it. The verse before it addresses “the virgin of Israel” and tells her to turn again to her cities, so the new thing is spoken to her; the verses quoted do not link the two. Possible readings, named only as readings: a new protection or safe return of the people; a reversal of roles between the people and what surrounds them; an image of something yet to come. The record does not decide between them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to the two verses quoted. The record does not say that any reading is the right one and does not claim that no other passage says more. The Greek prints this verse differently from the KJV; that is a separate record.

sides.label: A
sides.quote: the Lord hath created a new thing in the earth, A woman shall compass a man

title: “The Lord thy God hath pronounced this evil upon this place” — how does the captain of the guard know?
summary: In Jeremiah 40:2–3 the captain of the guard of the king of Babylon speaks to Jeremiah of what “the Lord thy God” pronounced and “hath brought”. The verses quoted do not say how he came to know of it.
text: KJV Jeremiah 39:11: “Now Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon gave charge concerning Jeremiah to Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, saying,” KJV Jeremiah 40:2: “And the captain of the guard took Jeremiah, and said unto him, The Lord thy God hath pronounced this evil upon this place.” KJV Jeremiah 40:3: “Now the Lord hath brought it, and done according as he hath said: because ye have sinned against the Lord, and have not obeyed his voice, therefore this thing is come upon you.”
reasoning: The captain is introduced in 39:11 as the officer to whom the king of Babylon gave charge concerning Jeremiah. In 40:2–3 he says that the Lord pronounced the evil and has done it “according as he hath said” because the people sinned and “have not obeyed his voice”. The verses quoted do not say whether he had this from Jeremiah’s words, from the people of Judah, or from some other source, and they do not say whether he is repeating what he was told or speaking his own mind. Possible readings, named only as readings: he had heard Jeremiah’s message; he had heard it from those he had taken captive; he is using the language of the people he has taken. The record does not decide between them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to the three verses quoted. The record does not say that any reading is the right one, does not rest on the Hebrew or the Greek, and does not claim that no other passage says more about the captain.

sides.label: A
sides.quote: The Lord thy God hath pronounced this evil upon this place

title: “Baalis the king of the Ammonites hath sent Ishmael to slay thee” — why did Ishmael kill Gedaliah?
summary: Jeremiah 40:14 says Baalis king of the Ammonites sent Ishmael to slay Gedaliah, and 41:2 reports that Ishmael did. The verses quoted do not say why Baalis wanted it done or why Ishmael did it.
text: KJV Jeremiah 40:14: “And said unto him, Dost thou certainly know that Baalis the king of the Ammonites hath sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to slay thee? But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam believed them not.” KJV Jeremiah 41:2: “Then arose Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and the ten men that were with him, and smote Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan with the sword, and slew him, whom the king of Babylon had made governor over the land.” KJV 2 Kings 25:25: “But it came to pass in the seventh month, that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, the son of Elishama, of the seed royal, came, and ten men with him, and smote Gedaliah, that he died, and the Jews and the Chaldees that were with him at Mizpah.”
reasoning: Jeremiah 40:14 names the sender, Baalis, and the man sent, Ishmael, and Gedaliah does not believe it (40:16). Jeremiah 41:2 says Ishmael killed “him, whom the king of Babylon had made governor over the land”, and 2 Kings 25:25 says Ishmael was “of the seed royal”. None of the verses quoted says what either of them wanted. Possible readings, named only as readings: a claim of the royal line against a governor Babylon had set; the interest of the Ammonite king; opposition to the Babylonian governor as such. The record does not decide between them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to the three verses quoted. The record does not say that any reading is the right one, does not rest on the Hebrew or the Greek, and does not claim that no other passage says more about Baalis or Ishmael.

sides.label: A
sides.quote: Baalis the king of the Ammonites hath sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to slay thee
